360: Outside this range the inclination angle is not constant. We found
361: i$=$66.1$\degr$ $\pm$ 0.8$\degr$ and i$=$68.4$\degr$ $\pm$
362: 0.6$\degr$ for the approaching and receding sides respectively.
363: Finally, we have determined the position angles separately for the
364: two sides of the galaxy. The mean values (obtained by averaging
365: over the whole galaxy) for the inclination and the position angles
366: are 67.2$\degr$ $\pm$ 0.6$\degr$ and -37.0$\degr$ $\pm$
367: 1.4$\degr$, respectively. 
368: 
369: Using the values found for the inclination and position angles, we
370: have determined the rotation curve first for the two sides of the
371: galaxy separately and then for the whole galaxy (Fig.
372: \ref{rotcur}). As already noted, NGC\,4559 is kinematically
373: lopsided. The rotation curves of the two sides of the galaxy are
374: significantly different. The rotation curve of the approaching
375: side rises to 110 km s$^{-1}$ inside 5 kpc and subsequently
376: flattens, while on the receding side it continues to rise out to
377: the outer parts where it reaches 123 km s$^{-1}$. This can also be
378: seen in the velocity field, where the isovelocity contours are
379: more curved on the approaching S-E side (see Figure 1).

394: In the Appendix we present two mass models for NGC\,4559. The
395: maximum disk fit gives a mass-to-light ratio M/L=0.27 in K-band.
396: In order to determine the error bars of the rotation curve in
397: Fig.\ref{rotcur_anom} and Fig. \ref{isot}, we have
398:  constructed a residual velocity field by subtracting a model from
399: the observed velocity field.
400: Then, we have taken the mean values along ellipses defined by the position
401: and the inclination angles obtained from the tilted-ring model analysis.
402: In this way the error bars give also a measure of the deviations from
403: circular motion.
